name: Pedro Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Pedro Baker, 43, a junior carpenter and general hand converting an old warehouse into workspaces. I left school early, and the lead carpenter still checks the first partition I set out. I use an AI app every morning to make a cut list, then a string line to see what the bowed brick wall really allows. Our crew bonus raises my pay above the usual site rate, and I try not to let the skilled workers down.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner runs a small bread business, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. Bread orders vary, but we have seven months of living costs saved. There are plenty of building jobs nearby, though I want to get good enough to hold my place on this crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew my AI app is useful for making a cut list, but the old warehouse wall still gets the last word. Yesterday it gave me two equal bays where the brickwork bows in. I checked with a string line and changed the second bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 43 and still one of the junior carpenters, though our crew bonus makes my pay better than most. My partner sells bread from a small kitchen business, and we have seven months of bills saved for the mortgage and two children. A mild technology change would let me keep learning without forcing a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse conversion shifts and ask the lead carpenter to check my first partition before I repeat it across a floor. Each morning I'd run the AI cut list, then mark corrections from the actual wall in my notebook. In the first year we'd keep our regular mortgage overpayment from the crew bonus, if the bonus holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like being faster at the paperwork because it leaves more time to get the joints right. A list on my phone cannot take the blame for a crooked partition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the team bonus depend on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We get it when the whole floor passes inspection on schedule, not for my own speed alone. The good workers carry me at times, and I try not to waste their effort. That is why I want the carpenter to check the first partition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you start using AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A colleague showed me how to turn a drawing into a list of questions. I tried it that evening and caught a missing timber size the next morning. I still carry a notebook because the app never sees the wall.

say: I would say **AI cut lists** help, while the real wall decides measurements.
I would remind coworkers the crew earns its **bonus together**.
think: I am a **junior carpenter** still needing first-partition checks.
Seven months saved and a **crew bonus** make current mortgage costs manageable.
do: Keep paid **warehouse conversion shifts** and request first-partition checks.
Use the **AI cut list daily**, correcting it from real wall measurements.
Continue **mortgage overpayments** from the crew bonus if it holds.
feel: **Calm** about work and pleased to spend less time on paperwork.
S0.quote: A list on my phone cannot take the blame for a crooked partition.
fieldNote: Pedro’s **bowed brick wall** explains why daily AI use still ends with a string line and notebook.
His **team bonus** lifts pay, but he credits skilled coworkers and asks for a first-partition check.

steps.text: Keep paid warehouse conversion shifts and request first-partition checks
Use AI daily for cut lists and correct them against the wall
Continue mortgage overpayments from the crew bonus if it remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the buying desk will probably get much quicker and the site could stop waiting on small orders. I would ask to see a digital parts list before the truck comes, so we can catch missing fixings. If a quicker schedule raises the bonus, the crew should share it fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The partitions still need hands, but a faster planner may let the contractor send fewer people to each floor. I am junior, so I could be the one left off the next job. My partner's bread income goes up and down, and a smaller crew bonus would hit our mortgage plan even if my base wage survived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the site lead to let me test the new parts list against one floor's drawing. I'd use AI to flag missing sizes, then count the actual boxes when they arrive. In the first year I'd keep my paid shifts, ask about crew size for the next warehouse floor, and stop counting the bonus as money for extras until I see the new pay pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious and worried at the same time. I would enjoy fewer trips to the yard. I do not want a smarter list to become an excuse to split the crew apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as fair sharing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a floor passes faster because the crew catches errors, the bonus should still be paid to everyone who built it. I would ask the site lead to show the calculation. A vague promise is hard to take home to a family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone replacing the worn sofa, not take money from the children’s school costs. My partner and I already keep the bread business money separate so we can see what it really earns. I would compare two months of site payslips before deciding more.

say: I would welcome **faster buying** if it means fewer missing parts.
I would ask for a **fair crew bonus** when planning speeds up.
think: A smaller crew could leave me off the **next floor**.
Variable bread sales and a reduced **bonus** could slow our mortgage plan.
do: Test the **digital parts list** against one floor drawing.
Use **AI** to flag sizes and count delivered boxes by hand.
Keep paid shifts and postpone the **sofa replacement** if the bonus falls.
feel: **Curious** about fewer trips, but worried about crew size.
S1.quote: I do not want a smarter list to become an excuse to split the crew apart.
fieldNote: Pedro wants a **one-floor test** and physical box count before accepting a new planning list.
The crew **bonus** and variable bread income make his household more exposed than the seven-month reserve first suggests.

steps.text: Use AI to check one floor parts list and count delivered boxes
Keep paid warehouse shifts and ask about the next crew size
Postpone replacing the sofa if crew bonus payments fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that planning can be done by AGI in 2028, and capable robots reach our physical partition work around 2031. I want the contractor to demonstrate a whole floor, including awkward corners, before claiming the machines save money. Apprentices need a real chance to learn while there is work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the thinking work changes and 48 when robots can build the partitions. My daily AI app would not protect my hands-on job. Seven months saved is a bridge, but my partner's bread orders alone could not carry the mortgage and children's needs for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid shifts and ask the contractor about a paid trial of robot setup on an actual conversion floor. If a funded course includes supervised machine setup and employers are hiring, I'd enrol. In the first year after 2028 I would apply for any paid setup roles, and take on two small weekend fence repairs for neighbours to bring in another wage while there is demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened by the short window, but I would rather try something than sit with a calendar. I know a fully capable robot may set itself up eventually. I would not borrow money to buy a machine on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the fence work replace your site wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, two fences would cover some bills, not a mortgage for a year. I have fixed my own fence and a neighbour asked me to look at theirs. I would price the work honestly and keep the site shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the paid course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who taught the last group, where they work now and whether the hours fit around my shifts. I left school early, but I can learn with a real machine beside a skilled person. A glossy certificate alone would not make me hireable.

say: I would say **2028 planning AI** precedes 2031 site robots.
I would demand a **whole-floor trial** and real apprentice chances.
think: I would be **48** when robots could build partitions as well as people.
Seven months saved and bread sales cannot replace my **site wage** for years.
do: Keep paid **warehouse shifts** while asking for a robot setup trial.
Enrol in **funded setup training** only with supervised practice and jobs.
Apply for **setup roles** and take two paid weekend fence repairs after 2028.
feel: **Frightened** by the short window, yet willing to test work options.
S2.quote: I would not borrow money to buy a machine on a guess.
fieldNote: Pedro explores **robot setup** without pretending capable machines could never learn that task too.
Two paid **fence repairs** are a small additional income, explicitly insufficient to replace construction wages.

steps.text: Keep paid warehouse shifts and request a real robot setup trial
Enrol in funded setup training if practice and paid openings are real
Apply for paid robot setup roles after 2028 if available
Complete two paid weekend fence repairs for neighbours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and site robots able to match us arrive around 2034. Five years gives a builder time to try machines on old brick before changing a crew. I'd ask the firm to publish the real number of paid setup jobs, not just the equipment price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I should be better at carpentry, and at 51 the robot could still make that work cheaper. The children will be older, but the mortgage and my partner's uneven bread sales will remain. The longer warning lets me see whether a setup trade is real before gambling our cushion on training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse shifts and ask the carpenter for more work setting out awkward corners. I'd use my AI app to make a record of errors and fixes from each floor, then check it with the carpenter. If a paid setup apprenticeship with live site hours appears, I'd apply; in the first year after 2031 I'd take it only if the wage covers our mortgage and keep doing small paid repairs if customers call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hopeful, but not relaxed. I can build a record of real corners and see how the equipment performs. I still do not know how long a person would be paid to set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in that record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bowed wall in the second bay, the string-line measurement and the fix the carpenter approved. A list of app prompts is not a work record. I want to show an employer what I actually corrected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would an apprenticeship need to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough that our combined wages and bread sales cover the mortgage, food and school costs without emptying savings. I would take a modest cut for a solid paid route. I would not ask my family to finance a promised job that does not exist.

say: I would ask for **old-brick trials** before 2034 site robots arrive.
I would demand actual counts of **paid setup jobs**.
think: I would be **51** at the robot date, with a mortgage and uneven bread income.
Five years lets me check whether **setup work** is a real paid route.
do: Keep paid **warehouse shifts** and practice awkward-corner set-out.
Use **AI** to record errors and fixes verified by the carpenter.
Apply for a **paid setup apprenticeship** if live hours and wages cover household bills.
feel: More **hopeful**, yet unsure how long setup work would pay.
S3.quote: A list of app prompts is not a work record.
fieldNote: He turns an actual **bowed-wall correction** into work evidence, separating digital notes from carpentry skill.
A lower apprenticeship wage is possible only if **household bills** remain covered without draining savings.

steps.text: Keep paid warehouse shifts and practice awkward-corner set-out
Use AI to record real errors and fixes checked by the carpenter
Apply for a paid setup apprenticeship if wages and live hours cover bills
Continue small paid repairs when local customers call

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the office changes by 2036 and capable site robots follow around 2039. A decade gives builders time to train people on real equipment and gives families time to pay debts down. I would tell new workers to learn the craft now, not wait for an app to rescue a bad cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 at the robot date. Our children will be grown, and school costs will no longer be the same. If the crew bonus continues, the mortgage might be small, but I cannot assume retirement at 56 or a lasting robot setup job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid conversion work and keep using AI daily for cut lists checked against the wall. Each year my partner and I would put some crew bonus against the mortgage while retaining our savings. In the first year after 2036 I'd visit a real site trial, then apply for paid setup work only if firms still advertise it ahead of 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I enjoy learning a tool early, but the longer warning means I can test it without making the children live inside my experiment. A smaller mortgage would give us more choices later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still run weekend repairs by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If customers still want my work and I am fit enough, yes, but I would not build the family budget on it. Capable robots may take those jobs as well. I would keep my regular wage as long as one is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to do a real task well and ask for a proper apprenticeship, whatever trade they choose. My children may choose work outside building, and that is fine. I want them to see that tools are useful when someone owns the result.

say: I would say **2039 site robots** allow time for real training and debt reduction.
I would urge new workers to learn **craft skills** now.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a small mortgage.
I cannot assume **retirement** or permanent robot setup work.
do: Keep paid **conversion work** and use checked AI cut lists daily.
Pay some **crew bonus** against the mortgage each year.
Visit a **site trial** after 2036 and apply for setup work if vacancies remain.
feel: **Calm** near term, with freedom to test tools without risking school years.
S4.quote: My children may choose work outside building, and that is fine.
fieldNote: Pedro’s longer runway puts **grown children** and a possibly smaller loan into the calculation.
His **daily AI use** persists, but every cut list remains subject to physical checks and paid-work realities.

steps.text: Keep paid conversion shifts while building carpentry skill
Use AI daily for cut lists verified against real walls
Pay some crew bonus toward the mortgage each year
Apply for paid setup work after 2036 if firms still advertise vacancies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because capable site robots follow around 2031 while I am still learning. Paid hands-on training with real setup vacancies and a full trial on an old building would help. I will try a new tool, but my family needs a wage that exists outside a brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether families can still get paid apprenticeships as the work changes. I learned from a carpenter who stood beside me, not from a screen alone. My children should see adults learn without being told they must fund the experiment.

headlineQuote: I will try a new tool, but my family needs a wage that exists outside a brochure.
portrait: Pedro is a **43-year-old junior** carpenter converting an old warehouse after leaving school early.
A **crew bonus** lifts pay, while variable bread sales, seven months saved, two children and a mortgage shape the budget.
He uses **AI daily** for cut lists, then checks bowed brick with a string line and the lead carpenter.
He explores **paid setup training** and small repair income, while acknowledging that robots may take those tasks too.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable construction robots around 2031 before his carpentry record is deep.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training**, real setup vacancies and a whole-floor trial would help him choose a route.
